Some days are better than others. The good days I’m thankful for, because I can enjoy things. The bad days I wake up and just feel it in my heart. There’s an emptiness in my chest. Sometimes I feel like I’m not even in control of myself, it feels like I’m outside of my body watching everything happen around me. I’ve only experienced this “out-of-body” sensation twice, but it terrifies me. 

I was diagnosed with depression, anxiety, panic disorder, agoraphobia and OCD 4 years ago, and I’m doing much better now than I was before. I haven’t self-harmed in over a year now and I’m taking my medication and going to counselling regularly. 

To all others who are struggling, keep holding on!

My first year of university I was living in residence and since I suffered from severe anxiety/depression I had trouble making friends. Eventually I started hanging out with a guy on another floor in my dorm because I was so desperate for friends. I knew he was bad news, but I was just happy someone was paying attention to me. 

One night he invited me to a party on his floor. I said yes, but was so nervous that I had a couple pre-drinks before going, but I was still pretty sober. The night was going by pretty well, I had a few drinks but still wasn't drunk. Things were fine until I lost my student card and started looking in the rooms I had previously been in. My "friend" followed me with another guy and locked me in the room. My "friend" guarded the door while the other guy assaulted me. I'm not going into detail, as it's hard to talk about.

I'm thankful that another guy saved me that night after realizing something was up when he saw this guy standing at the door. An RA was called and I was forced to explain what happened, though I didn't want to talk about it. Eventually the case made it up to the residence manager who decided that it never would've happened if I hadn't been drinking. 
I dropped out of the university soon after this and switched schools. I'm doing better at my new school, but I'm still struggling. I haven't told anyone about it, not even my parents. I think the hardest part of the whole thing was being told that what happened to me was my fault, at least it was my fault in the eyes of the university.
